summary: Two temporary lens-lantern lights on the Cape Vincent breakwater in 1901, wooden towers from 1904, steel structures from 1951; one wooden tower survives on Route 12E.

lens.note: LighthouseFriends says fifth-order Fresnel lenses were in the wooden towers when they were removed in 1951; the USLHS record gives the original optic as a lens lantern installed in 1901.

structures.note: Twin eleven-foot-square towers of 1904, 25 ft high (LighthouseFriends); the USLHS record gives 23 ft from base to lantern centre and dates the tower to 1901.

structures.type: steel skeletal structure with tank house
structures.note: Replaced the wooden towers in 1951 (LighthouseFriends); whether a light still shows from it is not stated in the sources read.

access.note: Grounds open, tower closed (LighthouseFriends). The USLHS record says the station is not open to the public.

visit.note: Stands alongside Route 12E (Market Street), near the Town of Cape Vincent highway department building.

events.note: Act of March 3, 1899 provided for a 1,400-foot timber crib breakwater parallel to the railroad wharf.
First section of the breakwater finished.
Two temporary fixed red lights established August 31, 1901 on the completed portion of the breakwater, shown from lens lanterns on masts.
Light-house structures for the Cape Vincent breakwater listed in the Board's engineering work for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1901.
Temporary lights replaced by twin eleven-foot-square wooden towers, 25 ft high, with lens lanterns showing fixed red.
Eastern tower moved 500 ft east onto concrete piers in November 1906.
500-foot cable lifeline on iron pipe posts installed along the breakwater for the keeper.
Halsey W. Crapo transferred to Cape Vincent.
Eastern light moved another 250 ft; the breakwater then measured 1,381 ft.
Efficiency flag awarded to the station under keeper Crapo (Bulletin index 1918-1923 p. 9; Bulletin 1918 p. 22). LighthouseFriends says the flag came in 1917 and again in 1927.
Keeper Halsey W. Crapo died June 5, 1929, while serving as keeper.
Illuminant changed from incandescent oil vapor to electricity on June 28, 1939.
Old wooden towers removed from the pier and replaced by white steel skeletal structures with tank houses.
USLHS gives 1951 as the year the station was discontinued; the disposition is listed as moved to park display.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's conflict list gives 1912 (Wikidata). The sources read for this story date the first lights to August 31, 1901 (LighthouseFriends; USLHS 1901; the Board's 1901 report lists the breakwater structures). No source read supports 1912.

USLHS dates the tower to 1901 (its tower-established year, which matches the first temporary lights). LighthouseFriends dates the twin wooden towers that replaced them to 1904. The surviving tower's identity (eastern or western tower, both moved) is not stated, so 1904 is the built date for the wooden tower in use.
LighthouseFriends gives 25 ft for the 1904 towers; USLHS gives 23 ft from base to lantern centre and 26 ft above mean high water for the light. The record's 7.0 m matches the 23 ft figure.

notes_for_editor: Dates for 1902 to 1906 (the $5,000 request, the 1904 wooden towers, the 1906 move) come from LighthouseFriends, which says the Lighthouse Board's reports for those years show no building. Those Board reports for 1902 to 1910 are not in the local corpus (the lhb series stops at fiscal 1901), so they are unverified here. The 1901 report sentence is OCR text (reads fructures for structures); it is quoted as printed. The roster and place record were matched by name and position (0.74 km); the USLHS position (44 07.54 N, 76 20.14 W) differs from the record's position by about 0.7 km, and the record's LighthouseFriends position was kept. The record's 1912 first-lit date and the Wikipedia infobox (Fifth Order Fresnel; 15 ft tower; 1912 first lit) were not used as sources. The Coast Guard Historian's page (USCG Cape Vincent Breakwater Lighthouse, archived copy at web.archive.org/web/20250117112304/...) gives Station Established 1900 in a search snippet, but the archived copy returned only the Wayback banner, so it is not cited. Whether a light still shows from the steel structures is not established by the sources read; the Coast Guard List of Lights was not consulted. The 1904 lawsuit reported by LighthouseFriends against the first keeper is a private matter and is left out. No wreck, storm or rescue at the breakwater light appears in the Life-Saving Service reports (1876-1909) in the corpus, where Cape Vincent appears only as a vessel's home port or in stranding tables without a place, so the Storms chapter is omitted. Newspaper search (Chronicling America, NY, 1901-1915) found nothing usable. The 1912 Watertown Daily Times headline and the 1904 Oswego Daily Palladium item are cited only as LighthouseFriends reports them, and neither was read directly. Most narrative facts rest on one secondary source (LighthouseFriends), backed by the Board's 1901 report, the USLHS record and the Bulletin for 1918 and 1929. Fact-check 2026-10-28: the Crapo link on Bulletin 1918 page 22 comes from an OCR'd keeper table, and Crapo is matched to the 10th district Cape Vincent entry by column position; the 1918-1923 index independently lists him against the Cape Vincent efficiency flag at page 22. The page image was not viewed because the PDF is not in the cache. The Hough wording is quoted from the LighthouseFriends page. The tower height is stated in the story as a disagreement: 25 ft (LighthouseFriends) against 23 ft from base to lantern centre (USLHS).
